blocks.p: But to return to our purpose. After the town had carried this news to Diabolus, and told him besides that the Prince, who lay encamped outside the wall, was waiting on them for an answer, he refused, and blustered as well as he could; but in his heart he was afraid.

“I will go down to the gates myself,” he said, “and give him such an answer as I think fit.” So he went down to Mouth-gate and there addressed himself to Emmanuel, though in a language the town did not understand. What he said was this:

“O great Emmanuel, Lord of all the world, I know you: you are the Son of the great Shaddai! Why have you come to torment me and to cast me out of my possession? This town of Mansoul, as you very well know, is mine, and by a double right. First, it is mine by right of conquest. I won it in the open field; and shall the prey be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captive be delivered? [Isa. 49:24] Second, this town of Mansoul is mine by their own submission. They opened the gates of their town to me; they swore loyalty to me and openly chose me as their king; they also gave their castle into my hands; yes, they have put the whole strength of Mansoul under me.

“Moreover, this town of Mansoul has disowned you. They have thrown your law, your name, your image, and everything that is yours behind their backs, and have accepted and set up in their place my law, my name, my image, and everything that is mine. Ask your captains if you doubt it, and they will tell you that in answer to all their summonses Mansoul has shown love and loyalty to me, but always disdain, spite, contempt, and scorn to you and yours. Now, you are the Just One and the Holy, and must do no wrong. Depart from me, then, I beg you, and leave me in peace to my just inheritance.”

This speech was made in Diabolus’s own language. For although he can speak to every man in his own tongue (otherwise he could not tempt them all as he does), he has a language of his own, and it is the language of the infernal cave, the black pit.
So the town of Mansoul (poor hearts!) did not understand him, nor did they see how he crouched and cringed as he stood before Emmanuel, their Prince.

Indeed, all this while they took him to be a power and force that could by no means be resisted. So while he was pleading to keep his residence there and not be driven out by force, the inhabitants were boasting of his valor, saying, “Who is able to make war with him?” [Rev. 13:4]
Well, when this pretended king had finished, Emmanuel, the golden Prince, stood up and spoke:

“You deceiver, I have something to say to you in my Father’s name, in my own name, and on behalf of and for the good of this wretched town of Mansoul. You claim a right, a lawful right, to the pitiable town of Mansoul, when it is perfectly plain to all my Father’s court that the entrance you gained at the gates of Mansoul came through your lie and falsehood. You lied about my Father, you lied about his law, and so you deceived the people of Mansoul. You claim that the people have accepted you as their king, their captain, and their rightful lord; but that too was done by deceit and cunning. Now, if lying, trickery, sinful craft, and every kind of horrible hypocrisy will pass for fairness and right in my Father’s court (and in that court you must be tried), then I will admit to you that you have made a lawful conquest. But alas, what thief, what tyrant, what devil is there who could not conquer in that way? I can make it plain, O Diabolus, that in all your claims to a conquest of Mansoul you have nothing true to say. Do you think it right that you put the lie on my Father, and made him out, to Mansoul, to be the greatest deceiver in the world? And what do you say to your knowingly twisting the true purpose and intent of the law? Was it good, too, that you made a prey of the innocence and simplicity of the now miserable town of Mansoul? Yes, you overcame Mansoul by promising them happiness in breaking my Father’s law, when you knew, and could not help knowing if you had consulted nothing but your own experience, that this was the way to ruin them. You have also, O master of enmity and spite, defaced my Father’s image in Mansoul and set up your own in its place, to the great contempt of my Father, the heightening of your sin, and the intolerable damage of perishing Mansoul.

“Moreover, as if all these were small things to you, you have not only deluded and ruined this place, but by your lies and fraudulent dealings you have set them against their own deliverance. How you have stirred them up against my Father’s captains, and made them fight against those he sent to free them from their bondage! All these things, and very many more, you have done against your own light, in contempt of my Father and his law, and with the design of bringing the miserable town of Mansoul under his displeasure forever. I have come, therefore, to avenge the wrong you have done my Father, and to deal with you for the blasphemies with which you have made poor Mansoul blaspheme his name. Yes, you prince of the infernal cave, I will repay it on your head.

“As for myself, O Diabolus, I have come against you by lawful power, to take this town of Mansoul by strength of hand out of your burning fingers. For this town of Mansoul is mine, O Diabolus, and by undoubted right, as all will see who diligently search the most ancient and most authentic records; and I will plead my title to it, to the confusion of your face.

“First, as for the town of Mansoul, my Father built it and fashioned it with his own hand. The palace in the midst of that town, too, he built for his own delight. This town of Mansoul is therefore my Father’s, and by the best of titles, and whoever denies the truth of this must lie against his own soul.
“Second, O master of the lie, this town of Mansoul is mine.
“1. It is mine because I am my Father’s heir, his firstborn, and the only delight of his heart. I have therefore come up against you in my own right, to recover my own inheritance out of your hand.

“2. But further, as I have a right and title to Mansoul by being my Father’s heir, so I have also by my Father’s gift. It was his, and he gave it to me. Nor have I at any time offended my Father, that he should take it from me and give it to you. Nor have I been driven, by going bankrupt, to sell my beloved town of Mansoul to you or to put it up for sale. Mansoul is my desire, my delight, and the joy of my heart.

“3. But Mansoul is mine also by right of purchase. I have bought it, O Diabolus; I have bought it for myself. Since it was my Father’s, and mine as his heir, and since I have also made it mine by a great purchase, it follows that by every lawful right Mansoul is mine, and that you are a usurper, a tyrant, and a traitor in holding it. And the reason for my purchase was this. Mansoul had trespassed against my Father, and my Father had said that in the day they broke his law they would die. Now, it is more possible for heaven and earth to pass away than for my Father to break his word. So when Mansoul had indeed sinned by listening to your lie, I stepped in and stood surety to my Father, body for body and soul for soul, pledging that I would make amends for Mansoul’s transgressions; and my Father accepted it. So when the appointed time came, I gave body for body, soul for soul, life for life, blood for blood, and so redeemed my beloved Mansoul.

“4. Nor did I do this by halves. My Father’s law and justice, which were both concerned in the penalty threatened against transgression, are now both satisfied, and well content that Mansoul should be set free.
“5. Nor have I come out against you today except by my Father’s command. It was he who said to me, ‘Go down and deliver Mansoul.’
“So let it be known to you, O fountain of deceit, and let it be known also to the foolish town of Mansoul, that I have not come against you today without my Father.”
“And now,” said the golden-headed Prince, “I have a word for the town of Mansoul.”
But as soon as it was heard that he had a word for the besotted town, the gates were double-guarded, and every man was forbidden to listen to him. So he went on and said:

“O unhappy town of Mansoul, I cannot help being moved with pity and compassion for you. You have accepted Diabolus as your king, and have become a nurse and servant of Diabolonians against your sovereign Lord. You opened your gates to him, but you have shut them fast against me. You gave him a hearing, but you have stopped your ears at my cry. He brought you your destruction, and you received both him and it; I have come to you bringing salvation, and you pay no attention to me. Besides, as if with sacrilegious hands, you have taken yourself, with everything of mine that was in you, and given it all to my foe, the greatest enemy my Father has. You have bowed and submitted yourselves to him; you have vowed and sworn yourselves to be his. Poor Mansoul! What shall I do with you? Shall I save you? Shall I destroy you? What shall I do with you? Shall I fall on you and grind you to powder, or make you a monument of the richest grace? What shall I do with you? Listen, therefore, town of Mansoul, listen to my word, and you shall live. I am merciful, Mansoul, and you will find me so. Do not shut me out of your gates.

“O Mansoul, neither my commission nor my inclination is to do you any harm. Why do you run so fast from your friend, and cling so close to your enemy? I would have you be sorry for your sin, it is true, because that becomes you; but do not despair of life. This great force is not here to hurt you, but to deliver you from your bondage and bring you back to your obedience.

“My commission, indeed, is to make war on Diabolus your king, and on all the Diabolonians with him. For he is the strong man armed who keeps the house, and I will have him out. His spoils I must divide, his armor I must take from him, out of his stronghold I must cast him, and I must make it a dwelling place for myself. [Luke 11:21-22] And this, O Mansoul, Diabolus shall know when he is made to follow me in chains, and Mansoul rejoices to see it.

“I could, if I put forth my might now, make him leave you and depart at once. But it is in my heart to deal with him in such a way that the justice of the war I make on him may be seen and acknowledged by all. He took Mansoul by fraud, and he keeps it by violence and deceit; and I will strip him bare and naked in the eyes of all who look on.
“All my words are true. I am mighty to save [Isa. 63:1], and I will deliver my Mansoul out of his hand.”

This speech was meant chiefly for Mansoul, but Mansoul would not hear it. They shut up Ear-gate, barricaded it, kept it locked and bolted, set a guard at it, and commanded that no Mansoulian should go out to him and no one from the camp be let in, so horribly had Diabolus bewitched them into doing his will against their rightful Lord and Prince. No man, no voice, no sound of any man belonging to the glorious host was to come into the town.

So when Emmanuel saw that Mansoul was so entangled in sin, he called his army together (since now his words too were despised) and sent a command throughout his whole host to be ready for the appointed time. Now since there was no lawful way to take Mansoul except by getting in at the gates, and at Ear-gate as the chief of them, he commanded his captains and commanders to bring their rams, their slings, and their men, and place them at Eye-gate and Ear-gate, in order to take the town.

When Emmanuel had made everything ready to give Diabolus battle, he sent once more to ask Mansoul whether they would yield peaceably, or whether they were still resolved to drive him to the utmost extremity. Then they, together with Diabolus their king, called a council of war and agreed on certain proposals to offer Emmanuel. The next question was who should carry them. Now there was in the town of Mansoul an old man, a Diabolonian, whose name was Mr. Won’t-bow, a stiff man in his ways and a great worker for Diabolus. So they sent him, with his words put into his mouth. When he came to Emmanuel’s camp, a time was appointed to hear him; and at that time, after a Diabolonian ceremony or two, he began:

“Great sir, so that all men may know how good-natured a prince my master is, he has sent me to tell your lordship that rather than go to war he is very willing to hand over into your hands one half of the town of Mansoul. I am therefore to ask whether your Mightiness will accept this proposal.”
“The whole is mine by gift and by purchase,” said Emmanuel, “so I will never lose one half.”
Then Mr. Won’t-bow said, “Sir, my master has said that he will be content for you to be Lord of all in name and title, if he may possess only a part.”
Emmanuel answered, “The whole is mine in reality, not in name and word only. So I will be the sole Lord and possessor of all of Mansoul, or of none of it at all.”

Then Mr. Won’t-bow said again, “Sir, see how my master stoops! He says he will be content if only he may have some place in Mansoul assigned him to live in privately, and you shall be Lord of all the rest.”

Then the golden Prince said, “All that the Father gives me will come to me, and of all that he gives me I will lose nothing [John 6:37, 39], no, not a hoof nor a hair. So I will not grant him even the smallest corner of Mansoul to live in. I will have it all for myself.”

Then Won’t-bow said again, “But sir, suppose my lord should resign the whole town to you, with only this condition: that sometimes, when he comes into this country, he may be entertained as a passing traveler, for old acquaintance’ sake, for two days, or ten days, or a month or so. May not this small matter be granted?”

“No,” said Emmanuel. “He came as a passing traveler to David, and did not stay long with him, and yet it nearly cost David his soul. I will not consent that he should ever have any lodging there again.”

Then Mr. Won’t-bow said, “Sir, you seem very hard. Suppose my master should yield to all that your lordship has said, provided that his friends and relatives in Mansoul may have liberty to trade in the town and to keep their present homes. May not that be granted, sir?”

“No,” said Emmanuel. “That is contrary to my Father’s will. For all Diabolonians of every kind, those who are in Mansoul now and any who shall at any time be found there, shall lose not only their lands and liberties but their lives as well.”

Then Mr. Won’t-bow said again, “But sir, if he hands everything over to you, may not my master and great lord keep up some kind of old friendship with Mansoul, by letters, by travelers passing through, by chance opportunities, and the like?”

Emmanuel answered, “No, by no means. For any such fellowship, friendship, intimacy, or acquaintance, kept up in any way, form, or manner whatever, will tend to corrupt Mansoul, to turn their affections away from me, and to endanger their peace with my Father.”

Mr. Won’t-bow went further still. “But great sir,” he said, “since my master has many friends in Mansoul, and those dear to him, may he not, if he departs from them, out of his own generosity and good nature, give them as he sees fit some tokens of the love and kindness he had for them? Then Mansoul, when he is gone, may look on these tokens from their old friend and remember him who was once their king, and the merry times they used to enjoy together while he and they lived in peace.”

“No,” said Emmanuel. “For if Mansoul comes to be mine, I will not allow or consent that the least scrap, shred, or speck of dust of Diabolus be left behind as tokens or gifts given to anyone in Mansoul, to call to mind the horrible communion there was between them and him.”

“Well, sir,” said Mr. Won’t-bow, “I have one thing more to propose, and then I have come to the end of my commission. Suppose that, when my master has gone from Mansoul, someone still living in the town should have business of such high concern that if it were neglected he would be ruined; and suppose, sir, that nobody could help in that case as well as my master and lord. May not my master be sent for on so urgent an occasion as that? Or if he may not be let into the town, may not he and the person concerned meet in one of the villages near Mansoul, and there put their heads together and consult about the matter?”

This was the last of the ensnaring proposals Mr. Won’t-bow had to make on behalf of his master Diabolus; but Emmanuel would not grant it. “No case, or thing, or matter can arise in Mansoul, once your master is gone, that cannot be resolved by my Father,” he said. “Besides, it would be a great slight on my Father’s wisdom and skill to allow anyone from Mansoul to go out to Diabolus for advice, when they have already been told to make their requests known to my Father in everything, by prayer and supplication. [Phil. 4:6] Further, if this were granted, it would be granting that a door be left open for Diabolus and the Diabolonians in Mansoul to hatch and plot and carry out treasonable designs, to the grief of my Father and me, and to the utter destruction of Mansoul.”

When Mr. Won’t-bow had heard this answer, he took his leave, saying that he would carry word of the whole affair to his master. So he went back to Diabolus in Mansoul and told him everything: how Emmanuel would not allow, no, not by any means, that once Diabolus had gone out he should ever again have anything to do in Mansoul, or with anyone in it.

When Mansoul and Diabolus had heard this account, they agreed with one consent to do their utmost to keep Emmanuel out, and they sent old Dwell-on-it, of whom you have heard before, to tell the Prince and his captains so. The old gentleman came up to the top of Ear-gate and called to the camp for a hearing; and when it was given, he said, “I have orders from my high lord to bid you tell your Prince Emmanuel that Mansoul and their king are resolved to stand and fall together, and that it is useless for your Prince to think of ever having Mansoul in his hand, unless he can take it by force.”

So some went and told Emmanuel what old Dwell-on-it, a Diabolonian in Mansoul, had said. Then the Prince said, “I must try the power of my sword. For in spite of all the rebellions and rebuffs that Mansoul has made against me, I will not raise my siege and depart, but will surely take my Mansoul and deliver it from the hand of her enemy.” And with that he gave out a command that Captain Boanerges, Captain Conviction, Captain Judgment, and Captain Execution should march up to Ear-gate at once, with trumpets sounding, colors flying, and shouting for the battle. He wanted Captain Credence to join them as well. Emmanuel also gave orders that Captain Good-Hope and Captain Charity should draw themselves up before Eye-gate. He told the rest of his captains and their men to take up the best positions they could against the enemy all around the town. And everything was done as he had commanded.
